title: Wildcard Matching
description: Match a whole string against a pattern with ? for one character and * for any run of characters.
statement:
A file-sync tool decides whether a file name matches a pattern such as `*.log` or `backup-??.tar`. Write `wildcard_match(text, pattern)` that returns `True` when the **whole** of `text` matches `pattern`:

- `?` matches exactly one character, any character.
- `*` matches any run of characters, including an empty one.
- Every other character matches only itself, case-sensitively (`[` and `]` are ordinary characters too).
- There is no escape syntax: a `*` or `?` inside `text` is an ordinary character, which a `?` or `*` in the pattern can match.

**Examples**

```python
wildcard_match("report.pdf", "*.pdf")              # True
wildcard_match("backup-07.tar", "backup-??.tar")   # True
wildcard_match("report.pdf", "*.txt")              # False
wildcard_match("", "***")                          # True, a star can match nothing
```

Trying every way to place the stars is exponential. Aim for O(len(text) · len(pattern)) or better.
hints: Try small cases by hand. `?` is easy. What makes `*` hard is that you do not know how many characters it should swallow. What are your choices when you meet one?

Think of pairs (position in the text, position in the pattern): the answer for one pair depends on a few neighbouring pairs, so you can fill a table. Or remember only the last star you saw, and whenever the match fails let that star swallow one more character and retry.

Never retry from scratch: placing every star in every possible way is exponential on `*a*a*a*a*b`. And check for `*` in the pattern before you compare characters, so that a `*` inside the text is not matched like an ordinary character.
explanation:
**The idea.** `?` is easy: it consumes one character. `*` is the hard part, because you do not know how many characters it should swallow. The key observation is that you never need to reconsider an *earlier* star once a later one has been placed: if the rest of the text can be matched at all, the earlier star could have swallowed less and left the work to the later one. So remember only the most recent star and where its match currently ends.

**The loop.** Walk both strings. On a `*` in the pattern, remember its position and the current text position, and first assume it matches nothing. On a matching character (or `?`), advance both. On a mismatch, if there was a star, let that star swallow one more character of the text and retry from just after it; with no star, the match has failed. When the text is used up, only stars may be left in the pattern.

**Why not try everything.** Placing every star in every possible way is exponential: `*a*a*a*a*b` against a long string of `a`s explores an astronomical number of combinations and finds none. The same blow-up hits a naive translation into a regular expression.

**Complexity.** O(len(text) · len(pattern)) in the worst case, usually close to linear, with O(1) extra space. The dynamic-programming alternative fills a table `match[i][j]`, "do the first i characters of the text match the first j characters of the pattern?", in O(n·m) time. Its recurrence is simple and it is easier to get right the first time.

**Usual mistakes.** Comparing characters before checking for `*` (a `*` inside the text would then be matched like an ordinary character), forgetting that trailing stars match the empty string, and reaching for `fnmatch`, which gives `[` and `]` a meaning of their own.
